paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Stone took place at Mears, Colorado, in late August 1881, when armed men searched for Stone, a man suspected of killing a man named McCorkey, with the stated intention of lynching him.
Officials who had arrested Stone moved him away from a group of the dead man's friends, and no report in the coverage shows that the searchers found or harmed him.
A Denver News dispatch about the threat ran in papers from California to Maine, while a later letter from Mears identified the dead man as Edward McClarkey and did not mention a mob.
Mears was a small town on the Denver and Rio Grande railroad, about six miles above Poncho Springs.
According to the local letter, the dead man, Edward McClarkey, worked as a teamster for the Hudson Constructing company on the railroad and was described as "a steady quiet hard working man."

The same letter said that suspicion fell on four people it called "notorious characters" who had been in the town for several months: two women, C. A. Powers and Lizzie Wendall, and two men, Charles Conn and Charley Stone.
The body was found at Mears on Wednesday night, August 24, according to the wire reports and the local letter.
A coroner's inquest drew little testimony, and only after the witnesses had been discharged was the body found to have been shot through the region of the heart.

The Denver News special from South Arkansas said the evidence "points strongly" to Stone, whom it called "a notorious desperado," and that he had come over to South Arkansas after the killing and was arrested on the way.
A number of McCorkey's friends then came after him, but, in the dispatch's words, "the officials spirited him away."
That night fifty armed men were reported "scouring the streets" for Stone "with the intention of lynching him," though several versions of the same telegram said they were scouring "the country."

The local letter gave a different account of the arrest: the four suspects boarded an eastbound train, an extra train was sent after them, and they were overhauled at Salida and taken to the Buena Vista jail.
No report in the coverage shows that the armed men reached Stone, and the local letter, written three days after the killing, placed him in the Buena Vista jail.
The writer said the people of Mears "are rejoiced at their departure," and reported that the women's "bagnio" burned on August 27 in what it called "a spontaneous combustion."
About one hundred people followed McClarkey's body to burial above the town the same day.
No report of an indictment or trial of Stone or Conn was found.

The story reached most readers as a single telegram from Denver, credited to the Denver News's South Arkansas correspondent and carried on August 26 by papers in Sacramento, Washington, Memphis, Rock Island, Gold Hill, Cheyenne and Yankton.
It ran again on August 27 and 28 in Augusta, Memphis, Salt Lake City, Wheeling, Washington and Eureka, and as late as August 30 in the Butte Weekly Miner, which datelined it a "South Park special."

Headlines centered on the threat rather than the killing: the Sacramento Daily Record-Union ran "Lynchers Searching for the Murderer," the Evening Star "Looking for a Murderer to Lynch Him," and the Eureka Daily Sentinel "Want to Lynch Him."
The telegram presented the suspicion against Stone and the mob's purpose without comment, and none of the papers named the race of Stone or of the dead man.

The Fremont County Record's correspondent at Mears wrote in a different register, calling the suspects "villianous" and "desperate characters" and reporting the inquest, the arrest at Salida and the funeral, but not the armed search.

The wire spelled the dead man's name McCorkey, with variants McCorker, McCorky and McCarkey, while the local letter gave Edward McClarkey; the local, named correspondent is likely the better source for the name.
The wire said Stone alone was arrested on the way to South Arkansas, while the local letter said Stone, Conn and two women were taken at Salida from a train and jailed at Buena Vista.
